2.text: described as sitting in the sleeping-room, working with her needle on new

3.text: clothes of spotted skins, the best of their kind. No man ever sees her face,

4.text: which is said to be so bright and beautiful that whoever looks on it is in

5.text: danger of dying from the “lustful trembling of his loins.” She walks only on

6.text: skins. In the night-time, when she goes out for a walk, the best soft skins

7.text: are spread on the ground under her tiny feet. When taken along by the

8.text: bridegroom, she cannot travel on foot, because, being of a rich family, she

9.text: has been accustomed to drive reindeer, “even when going out to follow the

10.text: demands of nature.” All this, of course, does not correspond to the details

11.text: of Chukchee life, which is so plain, filthy, and democratic.

12.text: In some of these tales the bride is described as kept in a big iron box wit-

13.text: hout a lid. The suitor has to find the entrance, or to open the box and free the

14.text: prisoner. The parents usually do not want to give away their daughter, and

15.text: meet the suitor with much harshness. They invite him to perform many

16.text: difficult and perilous tasks, some of which are of shamanistic character, while

17.text: others are curiously akin to those really imposed upon Chukchee suitors. One

18.text: of the most frequently occurring tasks is the request to bring fuel from the

19.text: woods. In the tale of Attɪhɪˊtkɪ and his companions, the hero and his cousin

20.text: come to the house of a mighty man, whose name is Earth, to ask for his

21.text: daughter. Numerous suitors are in the house. They are Sun, Moon, Heaven,

22.text: Darkness, World, Sunrise, Sunset. After dinner the master says, “Our fuel

23.text: is at an end. Go and get some.” But it is difficult to find fuel. The country

24.text: is quite barren, except for one large trunk of a tree, as long as a river, which

25.text: stands in the middle of the sea. It is in constant motion. Now it is out of

26.text: the water, again it sinks down and is submerged. A strong keˊlᴇ is concealed

27.text: in the trunk of the tree. As soon as any one approaches with an axe and

28.text: wants to chop off wood, the tree shakes him down and thus causes him to

29.text: be drowned. Since all the suitors who have been sent are great shamans,

30.text: they rise from the waters on the opposite shore, and reach the house, following

31.text: the shore of the sea. Still none of them are able to get fuel from the tree.

32.text: The hero and his cousin succeed in deluding the watchfulness of the spirit.

33.text: They obtain a large quantity of wood, and carry it in triumph to the house

35.text: In other tales the parents conceal from the suitor the dwelling-place of

36.text: the bride. They visit her in the night-time. Still he finds the place, enters

37.text: in the darkness, and makes the girl his wife. She offers no resistance, and

38.text: is glad to have a husband. Then the parents have to give their consent.

39.text: Although it is more than probable that most of these details in the Chuk-

40.text: chee folk-tales are borrowed from more southern tribes, it is evident that they

41.text: were congenial to the character of the Chukchee, so that they became very
